title: Mirabai
hook: a holy man in Vrindavan won't meet a woman, and Mira sends him one sentence

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai with bells on her ankles, dancing while the town called her mad. Did some music get your foot tapping? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

A door, and a message passed through it. On one side, a learned renunciant in Vrindavan, a man who has made a rule for himself: he doesn't meet women. On the other side, a woman who has walked a long way to see him, and who has just been turned away. She doesn't argue about the rule. She sends back a single sentence. And by the end of the story, the door opens. The woman is Mira, and the sentence is today's whole lesson.
screen: `A DOOR, AND A MESSAGE.` → `A RULE: NO WOMEN.` → `ONE SENTENCE BACK.`

segments.voice: First, where she is. Tradition says that after the troubles with her husband's family, Mira left the palace and took to the road, and that she came to Vrindavan, the country of Krishna's childhood, where the cowherd girls, the gopis, once ran to the sound of his flute. Holy people and teachers lived there. The story names one of them as Jiva Goswami, a scholar of Krishna devotion; some tellings name another teacher. Here's the story, in paraphrase. Mira asks to meet him. Word comes back: he has vowed not to see women. And Mira answers, roughly: I thought there was only one man in Vrindavan, Krishna. I didn't know anyone else here was claiming to be a man. The renunciant hears it, and comes out to meet her. It's a sharp answer, and it's funny. But underneath the wit is a teaching that belongs to Vrindavan itself. In the devotion Vrindavan is known for, the soul stands before Krishna the way the gopis did: as the beloved, waiting for him. Before him, no one is the man of the house. So the rule that kept her out rested on a difference that, in that place, she says doesn't count. Then notice what she doesn't do. She doesn't attack his vow, or his learning, or him. She takes the faith of the place more seriously than the rule does, and lets that speak. Last, the story isn't a record anyone wrote down at the door. It comes to us as one of the stories told about her, and it's remembered because it teaches something, the way a parable is.
screen: `MIRA COMES TO VRINDAVAN` · `A HOLY MAN WHO WON'T MEET WOMEN` · `ONLY ONE MAN IN VRINDAVAN` · `A STORY THAT TEACHES`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: setting the label down. Sit, and let the breath slow. Notice the labels you carry today: your job, your role at home, how other people see you. Name one quietly to yourself. Then, on an out-breath, set it down beside you, the way you'd put down a bag. For a few breaths, just be someone breathing, without a title. When the bell comes, you can pick it up again. If you pray, you can stand before God for a moment without it. The bell holds the time.
Mirabai. Turned away in Vrindavan by a holy man who wouldn't meet women, she answered that there was only one man there, Krishna. Today's word.
Your line: Mirabai. Today, if a door closes on you, try answering the way she did: without attacking anyone, and with what the place itself stands for. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Vrindavan remains a place of pilgrimage for Krishna devotees, and stories of Mira's time there are told alongside her songs in bhajan gatherings.

fork.setup: you're Mira. you've walked to Vrindavan, and a holy man sends word that he doesn't meet women. what do you do?
options: send back that there's only one man in Vrindavan.
wait outside until he gives in.
fork.reveal: she answers that she thought Krishna was the only man in Vrindavan, and the renunciant comes out to meet her.

original.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: Vrindavan, the land of Krishna's childhood, where tradition says Mira came.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mira's answer was just a clever comeback.
what it means: in the devotion Vrindavan is known for, the soul stands before Krishna as the gopis did, as the beloved, so the rule rests on a difference she says doesn't count there.
what a scholar hears: the tellings disagree on which holy man it was; the story is kept as a teaching, more like a parable than a record.

sources.ref: Hagiographical tradition of Mirabai: the meeting at Vrindavan (often told of Jiva Goswami)

notes: The Vrindavan meeting is told as tradition. Most tellings name Jiva Goswami; some name Rupa Goswami or another teacher. The script says 'some tellings name another teacher'; confirm.
Confirm the paraphrase of Mira's reply (that she thought Krishna was the only purusha in Vrindavan and all others gopis).
Chronology (whether Mira and Jiva Goswami could have met) is deliberately not discussed; a Keeper may want a note.
Gaudiya Vaishnava sensitivity: the story should not read as a put-down of Jiva Goswami; the script frames it as her answering from the faith of the place without attacking him. Check tone.
Original game uses Vrindavan (वृन्दावन) rather than Mira's name, since day 1356 used मीराबाई.

Editor: softened the sweeping 'every soul stands before Krishna' to the devotion Vrindavan is known for (teach and trapdoor); source ref no longer says 'many tellings'; varied the 'turn it' transitions.
